passage.title: Borrowing Umbrellas That Actually Come Back
passage.text:
Many train stations keep a basket of free umbrellas near the exit for commuters caught in sudden rain. The idea is generous, yet most stations face the same problem: within a few weeks, the basket is empty. People rarely steal the umbrellas on purpose; instead, once the sky clears, they simply forget to bring them back.

Two years ago, a commuter railway tried a small experiment at five stations. Rather than buying plain black umbrellas, it partnered with a local high school art club. Students painted bright patterns—such as river fish, autumn leaves, and yellow trains—on the handles and panels. Each umbrella also carried a short tag saying which station was waiting for it to "come home." Surprisingly, this design helped (21).

Over six months, more than eighty percent of the painted umbrellas were returned, compared with fewer than thirty percent before. Commuters said an umbrella with a hand-painted tag felt like a borrowed item from a neighbor rather than a disposable object. For the students, seeing their artwork travel through town on rainy evenings became (22). Several other stations have since asked schools along their lines to join the project.

passage.title: Notice About Locker Replacement
passage.text:
From: Sports Club Office
To: Pool and Gym Members
Subject: Men's and women's locker rooms next week

Dear members,
Thank you for using Midori Sports Club. On Monday, September 14, and Tuesday, September 15, workers will replace the old coin lockers in both the men's and women's changing rooms with new keyless lockers. During these two days, the swimming pool and changing rooms will be closed.

However, the second-floor fitness gym and running track will remain open as usual. Members who plan to use the gym on Monday or Tuesday should arrive already dressed in workout clothes, as changing spaces will not be available. Small valuables such as phones and keys can be stored in temporary boxes beside the second-floor staff desk.

If you currently rent a monthly private locker, please empty it completely before 8:00 p.m. this Sunday, September 13. Anything left inside will be moved to our office and kept in labeled bags for two weeks.

Thank you for your cooperation,
Midori Sports Club Office
passage.translation: みどりスポーツクラブ事務局からプール・ジム会員への連絡。9月14日月曜と15日火曜の2日間、男女更衣室の古いコインロッカーを暗証番号式の新しいロッカーに入れ替えるため、プールと更衣室を閉鎖する。ただし2階のフィットネスジムとランニングトラックは通常営業する。月曜・火曜にジムを利用する会員は更衣場所が使えないため運動着を着用して来館すること。携帯電話や鍵などの小さな貴重品は2階スタッフデスク横の仮設ボックスに預けられる。月極の個人ロッカーを契約中の人は9月13日日曜午後8時までに中身をすべて空にすること。残された荷物は事務室へ移し、名前札付きの袋で2週間保管する。

passage.title: Audio Descriptions at Live Theater
passage.text:
Going to see a live play is exciting partly because so much happens without words: an actor glances nervously at a clock, a door slowly opens at the back of the stage, or warm yellow light shifts to cold blue. For theatergoers who are blind or have low vision, however, these silent visual moments can make a story hard to follow if they rely on dialogue alone.

To bridge this gap, more theaters now offer "audio-described" performances. Audience members who request the service wear a lightweight earpiece connected to a small receiver. Sitting in a soundproof booth at the back of the hall, a trained describer watches the stage and speaks quietly into a microphone, slipping short phrases about costumes, facial expressions, and movements into the natural pauses between actors' lines.

Writing good audio description is more delicate than simply listing everything on stage. If a mystery character hides a key in a coat pocket, naming the key too early could spoil a surprise that sighted audience members discover only later. Conversely, saying too little leaves listeners confused when everyone else gasps or laughs. Describers therefore attend rehearsals in advance, consult directors, and time every sentence down to the second.

Some theaters have also introduced "touch tours" thirty minutes before the curtain rises. Visitors who use audio description are invited onto the stage to feel the texture of a velvet cape, examine a wooden prop sword, and walk across the set to understand the distance between rooms. When the play begins, a brief phrase like "she crosses to the oak table" immediately calls up a clear mental picture.

Actors and directors say preparing for these performances often sharpens their own craft as well. Explaining why a gesture or lighting change matters forces the creative team to think carefully about every visual choice on stage.
passage.translation: 生の演劇の魅力の一部は、時計を気にする視線や後ろでゆっくり開く扉、照明の色の変化など言葉のない動きにありますが、視覚に障害のある観客には台詞だけでは筋を追いにくい場面が生じます。その橋渡しとして「音声ガイド付き公演」を行う劇場が増えています。希望者は小型受信機と軽いイヤホンを着け、ホール後方の防音ブースから専門解説者が衣装や表情、動きを俳優の台詞の自然な合間に短い言葉で伝えます。良い解説は舞台上の全てを列挙するのとは異なり、謎の人物がポケットに鍵を隠す場面で早く言いすぎればネタバレになり、少なすぎれば周囲が笑ったり息をのんだりする理由が分かりません。そのため解説者は事前に稽古を見学し演出家と相談して秒単位で調整します。さらに開演30分前に舞台へ上がり衣装の手触りや小道具、部屋間の距離を確かめる「タッチツアー」を行う劇場もあり、本番中の短い描写でも鮮明なイメージが浮かびます。俳優や演出家にとっても、動きや照明の意味を言葉で確認することが舞台表現を磨く機会になっています。

items.prompt: Why must describers be careful when choosing what to say?
choices: Too much detail too early might spoil a surprise, while too little causes confusion.
Their microphones can only work for five minutes.
Directors forbid them from mentioning costumes.
Audience members dislike hearing actors' voices.
items.explanation: 早く言いすぎると驚きを台無しにし、少なすぎると観客が混乱するため。
distractorReasons: 第3段落の鍵の例と説明に一致。
マイクが5分しか使えないとはない。
衣装への言及は第2段落で行われている。
台詞の邪魔をしないよう合間に入れている。
items.translation: 解説者が言葉選びに慎重でなければならないのはなぜですか。

passage.title: Audio Descriptions at Live Theater
passage.text:
Going to see a live play is exciting partly because so much happens without words: an actor glances nervously at a clock, a door slowly opens at the back of the stage, or warm yellow light shifts to cold blue. For theatergoers who are blind or have low vision, however, these silent visual moments can make a story hard to follow if they rely on dialogue alone.

To bridge this gap, more theaters now offer "audio-described" performances. Audience members who request the service wear a lightweight earpiece connected to a small receiver. Sitting in a soundproof booth at the back of the hall, a trained describer watches the stage and speaks quietly into a microphone, slipping short phrases about costumes, facial expressions, and movements into the natural pauses between actors' lines.

Writing good audio description is more delicate than simply listing everything on stage. If a mystery character hides a key in a coat pocket, naming the key too early could spoil a surprise that sighted audience members discover only later. Conversely, saying too little leaves listeners confused when everyone else gasps or laughs. Describers therefore attend rehearsals in advance, consult directors, and time every sentence down to the second.

Some theaters have also introduced "touch tours" thirty minutes before the curtain rises. Visitors who use audio description are invited onto the stage to feel the texture of a velvet cape, examine a wooden prop sword, and walk across the set to understand the distance between rooms. When the play begins, a brief phrase like "she crosses to the oak table" immediately calls up a clear mental picture.

Actors and directors say preparing for these performances often sharpens their own craft as well. Explaining why a gesture or lighting change matters forces the creative team to think carefully about every visual choice on stage.

passage.title: Borrowing More Than Books
passage.text:
A small library wanted to attract residents who rarely borrowed books. Instead of expanding its shelves, it began lending useful household objects, including a sewing machine and a set of gardening tools. The staff hoped that residents could try an object before deciding whether to buy one. People could also borrow items they needed only occasionally.

At first, the library accepted almost every donated object. This created an unexpected problem. Some items were missing parts, while others required repairs that the staff could not perform. The service soon became difficult to manage. The library therefore introduced a rule: every object had to be inspected before it was accepted. (18), donations became easier to handle, even though the library received fewer of them.

Another concern was that borrowers might return objects late. The library considered charging large fines, but staff worried this would discourage people from trying the service. Instead, borrowers received a reminder a day before an item was due. If they needed more time, they could request an extension unless someone else was waiting. The library found that clear communication was (19).

The service is still small. Staff have not claimed that it will replace shopping or solve all the town's waste problems. However, residents have started discussing which objects could usefully be shared. For the library, one important result has been (20). People who had never met now exchange advice about using and repairing the objects they borrow.
passage.translation: ある図書館は読書以外の利用者を呼び込もうと、ミシンや園芸道具など家庭用品の貸出を始めました。購入前に試したり、時々しか使わない物を借りたりできます。最初はほぼすべての寄贈品を受け入れたため、部品不足や修理不能の物が集まり、管理が難しくなりました。受入前の点検を義務化すると、(18)、数は減っても扱いやすくなりました。返却遅延には高額罰金でなく前日通知と、次の予約がない場合の延長で対応し、明確な連絡が(19)と分かりました。小規模な制度で買物の代替や廃棄物問題の全面解決は主張していませんが、共有に役立つ物について住民が話し始めました。重要な成果は(20)で、初対面の人同士が使い方や修理の助言を交換しています。

passage.title: A Sign That Needed Testing
passage.text:
Visitors to a nature reserve were often confused at a junction where two walking paths separated. One route led to a lake, while the other climbed a steep hill. To solve the problem, the reserve installed a large map. The staff were confident that a detailed map would provide all the information visitors needed.

However, volunteers noticed that many people still asked for directions. They interviewed visitors and learned that the map included many small paths but did not clearly show where the viewer was standing. The additional detail had made the map (21). The staff had thought about the whole reserve, while visitors needed to make one immediate choice.

A designer suggested placing a simple sign at the junction. It showed two arrows, the names of the destinations, and the walking time for each route. Before installing the final sign, the staff tested a temporary version for two weekends. They asked volunteers to record how often visitors stopped to ask questions. The number fell considerably. (22), fewer people accidentally began the steep route.

The detailed map was not removed. It remained useful near the entrance, where visitors could plan a longer walk. The project showed that good information is not always the largest amount of information. What matters is (23). The same person may need a broad overview at the start of a visit and a short, clear instruction at a junction.
passage.translation: 自然保護区の分岐点で来訪者が迷うため、職員は詳しい大きな地図を設置しました。しかし質問は減りません。聞き取りでは、小道は多く載っているのに現在地が不明確でした。詳細の追加が地図を(21)していたのです。職員は保護区全体、来訪者は目の前の選択を考えていました。デザイナーは矢印二つ、行き先、所要時間だけの標識を提案。仮設版を2週末試し、質問回数が大幅に減りました。(22)、誤って急な道へ進む人も減りました。詳しい地図は不要になったわけでなく、長い散策の計画を立てる入口で活用されています。情報は多ければよいのでなく、(23)ことが重要です。同じ人でも入口では全体像、分岐では簡明な指示が必要になります。

passage.text:
From: Elena Brooks, Project Leader
To: Student Exhibition Team
Subject: Final arrangements

Dear team,
Thank you for preparing the exhibition on the history of our neighborhood. After looking through your work, the community center has agreed to lend us its main hall. This will allow us to display larger photographs than we could in the school corridor. However, the hall is available for only one weekend, so we must finish setting up by Friday evening and remove everything on Sunday after closing.

We originally planned to borrow display boards from the town office. Unfortunately, they are needed for another event. The center has offered lightweight stands instead. These cannot hold heavy objects, so please do not bring the old tools you collected. Use photographs of them, with short explanations of what they were used for. Your interviews with residents can still be played through the small speakers.

Please send your final captions to me by Monday. I will check them for unclear dates and names, not change your choice of topics. If a resident has asked not to be named, use a description such as "a former shop owner." passage.title: Keeping Track of City Trees
passage.text:
On a summer afternoon, a tree-lined street can feel quite different from a nearby road without shade. Trees also provide places for birds and insects to live. Yet city officials often have incomplete information about the trees they are responsible for. Paper records may be old, and different departments may keep separate lists. This can make it difficult to decide where care is most urgently needed.

In one city, a group of residents offered to help create a shared tree record. Volunteers walked along public streets and entered basic information into a mobile form. They recorded each tree's location, took a photograph, and noted visible signs of damage. They were not asked to judge whether a tree was safe. That decision remained the responsibility of trained specialists.

The first month produced thousands of entries, but some were unreliable. A tree near a street corner might be recorded by two teams, while a photograph taken from far away might show the wrong tree. Rather than simply count the entries, the project leader introduced a checking stage. Teams compared neighboring records, and specialists reviewed reports of possible disease. Each confirmed tree received a single identification number.

The resulting map changed how the city planned its work. Officials had previously responded mainly to requests from residents. However, some neighborhoods made many requests while others made few, even when their trees were in poor condition. The new record allowed officials to compare areas more fairly. It also revealed streets where there were very few trees at all.

The project did not mean that every neighborhood could immediately receive new trees. Planting requires money, and there must be enough space underground for roots as well as above ground for branches. In some streets, water pipes and cables limited the available space. Officials had to explain why a request could not always be accepted.

For volunteers, the main lesson was that collecting information was only the beginning. The value of the record depended on checking it, keeping it current, and using it to answer practical questions. The group now revisits a different area each month. Its members hope that a record built through public participation will remain useful because people understand both its purpose and its limits.
passage.translation: 木陰のある街路は暑い午後にも涼しく感じられ、生き物の場所にもなります。しかし行政の樹木記録は古く、部署ごとに分かれ、必要な手入れの優先順位をつけにくいことがあります。ある市では住民が所在地、写真、目に見える損傷を記録しました。安全性の判断は専門家に残しました。当初は重複や別の木の写真が混じったため、近隣記録の比較と専門家の確認を追加し、確認済みの木に一意の番号を付与しました。従来は住民の要望中心で、声の多い地域と少ない地域の偏りがありましたが、新記録でより公平に比較でき、木の少ない街路も分かりました。ただし費用や根・枝の空間、地下の配管やケーブルの制約があり、すべての希望地にすぐ植樹できません。住民にはその理由の説明が必要でした。情報の収集は出発点であり、点検・更新・実際の判断への活用が価値を決めます。住民は毎月地域を変えて再確認し、目的と限界を理解する参加者がいることで記録が役立ち続けると期待しています。

passage.title: Why Supermarkets Adjust Their Music
passage.text:
Shoppers rarely pay conscious attention to the music playing overhead while they push a cart down an aisle. Yet retail researchers have long studied how tempo and volume subtly shape behavior inside stores. Fast, energetic songs tend to make people walk more briskly, whereas slower instrumental tracks encourage customers to pause and examine shelves.

A regional grocery chain recently reconsidered its daytime playlist after receiving feedback from older residents and parents of young children. Many found the combination of bright lights, announcements, and upbeat pop songs exhausting. In response, the chain introduced "quiet mornings" twice a week, turning off promotional broadcasts and lowering music volume. (18), complaints dropped and weekday morning visits grew steadily.

Interestingly, staff members benefited just as much as shoppers. Cashiers and shelf stockers spend up to eight hours in the store, hearing the same loop of songs repeatedly. When the store switched to calmer, varied acoustic pieces during regular hours, employees reported feeling less fatigued at the end of a shift. This mattered because (19).

The chain did not eliminate lively music altogether; weekend afternoon sales events still feature brighter playlists. However, managers stopped treating background sound as mere filler. They learned that (20) can make an ordinary errand noticeably less stressful for everyone inside the building.
passage.translation: 買い物客は店内の音楽を意識することはまれですが、曲の速さや音量は行動に微妙な影響を与えます。速い曲は足取りを速め、ゆっくりした器楽曲は棚をじっくり見る行動を促します。ある地域のスーパーは高齢者や子育て世帯から「明るい照明と館内放送、賑やかな曲の重なりで疲れる」との声を受け、週2回の「静かな朝」を導入して宣伝放送を止め音量を下げました。(18)、苦情は減り平日の朝の利用者が着実に増えました。さらに8時間同じ曲を聴き続けるレジ係や品出し係も、通常時間帯の曲が穏やかで多様なアコースティック曲に変わったことで勤務後の疲労軽減を実感しました。これは重要で、なぜなら(19)からです。週末午後の特売では明るい曲も残しましたが、経営陣はBGMを単なる埋め草とみなすのをやめ、(20)が誰にとっても買い物の負担を減らすと学びました。

passage.title: Saving Seeds in School Gardens
passage.text:
Many elementary and junior high schools plant cherry tomatoes or sunflowers each spring using packets of commercial seeds. Students water the beds, harvest the crop in summer, and clear the plot in autumn. The next April, teachers buy fresh seed packets and repeat the cycle. While children learn how plants grow, they seldom see how one generation of plants produces the next.

A group of science teachers in Nagano decided to extend this lesson by teaching students to collect and store seeds from their own harvest. The task turned out to require more care than simply drying a few pods on a windowsill. If seeds were sealed in jars while still slightly damp, mold ruined them over winter. Students had to measure weight changes over several days to confirm that the seeds were dry enough. (21), the project connected biology with careful data recording.

The teachers also noticed an unexpected change in how students treated the garden in late summer. Plants that had finished fruiting were once pulled up right away because they looked untidy. Once students understood that seed pods needed weeks on the stem to ripen fully, they put up small explanatory signs rather than clearing the beds prematurely. Visitors learned that the brown stalks were (22).

Not every saved seed sprouted the following spring, and cross-pollination occasionally produced surprising shapes in pumpkins. Far from being failures, these variations sparked lively classroom questions about genetics. Passing labeled envelopes of seeds to the incoming grade gave students (23).
passage.translation: 多くの小中学校では毎年春に市販の種を買ってミニトマトやヒマワリを育て、秋に片づけて翌春また新しい種を買います。植物の成長は学べても世代がつながる仕組みは見えにくいままでした。長野の理科教員グループは収穫物から種を採取・保存する授業を始めましたが、窓辺で乾かすだけでは不十分で、少しでも湿気が残ると冬にカビが生えました。数日間の重量変化を測って乾燥を確かめる必要があり、(21)、生物の観察と丁寧なデータ記録が結びつきました。晩夏の畑の扱いも変わり、以前は見た目が悪いとすぐ抜いていた枯れ茎も、種が熟すのに数週間要ると分かると説明札を立てて残すようになり、来校者にも茶色い茎が(22)と伝わりました。翌春すべてが発芽するとは限らず交雑で珍しい形のカボチャもできましたが、それが遺伝への疑問を呼び、次の学年へ種袋を引き継ぐことで生徒は(23)を得ました。

passage.title: Saving Seeds in School Gardens
passage.text:
Many elementary and junior high schools plant cherry tomatoes or sunflowers each spring using packets of commercial seeds. Students water the beds, harvest the crop in summer, and clear the plot in autumn. The next April, teachers buy fresh seed packets and repeat the cycle. While children learn how plants grow, they seldom see how one generation of plants produces the next.

A group of science teachers in Nagano decided to extend this lesson by teaching students to collect and store seeds from their own harvest. The task turned out to require more care than simply drying a few pods on a windowsill. If seeds were sealed in jars while still slightly damp, mold ruined them over winter. Students had to measure weight changes over several days to confirm that the seeds were dry enough. (21), the project connected biology with careful data recording.

The teachers also noticed an unexpected change in how students treated the garden in late summer. Plants that had finished fruiting were once pulled up right away because they looked untidy. Once students understood that seed pods needed weeks on the stem to ripen fully, they put up small explanatory signs rather than clearing the beds prematurely. Visitors learned that the brown stalks were (22).

passage.title: Relocating the Career Talk Sessions
passage.text:
From: Career Guidance Office
To: Second-Year High School Students
Subject: Room changes and question cards for Friday's Career Day

Dear students,
This Friday afternoon, twelve graduates working in fields ranging from nursing to civil engineering will visit our school for Career Day. Because more students signed up for the architecture and healthcare sessions than Room 201 and Room 202 can safely seat, those two sessions have been moved to the audiovisual hall and the library reading room. All other sessions remain in their original classrooms; please check the updated map posted outside the staff room.

Each guest will speak for twenty minutes and then spend fifteen minutes answering student questions. Rather than calling on hands randomly, student moderators will group similar questions together so more topics can be covered. For this reason, please submit at least one question through the class link by Wednesday at 5:00 p.m.

You will attend two sessions during the afternoon. Leave your backpacks in your homeroom and bring only a pen, your notepad, and your indoor shoes. Taking photographs or recording audio during the talks is not permitted, as several speakers will share workplace examples that are not for public distribution.

Career Guidance Office
passage.translation: 進路指導室から高校2年生への連絡。今週金曜午後のキャリアデーには看護から土木工学まで12名の卒業生が来校する。建築と医療の分科会は201・202教室の安全定員を超える申込があったため、視聴覚ホールと図書館閲覧室へ変更。他の分科会は元の教室のままなので職員室前の更新マップを確認すること。各講師は20分講演の後、15分質疑応答を行う。その場で無作為に挙手を当てるのではなく、より多くの話題を扱えるよう生徒司会者が似た質問をまとめるため、水曜午後5時までにクラスのリンクから最低1問提出すること。午後に2つの分科会へ参加する。リュックはホームルームに置き、ペン・メモ帳・上履きのみ持参。職場内の非公開事例が含まれるため写真撮影や録音は禁止。

passage.title: Repair Cafes and How Products Are Designed
passage.text:
Across many cities, weekend "repair cafes" invite residents to bring broken toasters, lamps, and bicycles to community halls where skilled volunteers help fix them for free. Most visitors come with a practical goal: extending the life of a household item and keeping it out of the trash. Over the past decade, however, these grassroots gatherings have begun producing something else of value—detailed records of why everyday appliances fail.

Volunteers at dozens of repair groups log each item's brand, approximate age, and the specific fault they encountered. When thousands of entries are combined, clear patterns emerge. For example, a handheld vacuum might have a motor capable of running for ten years, yet be discarded after two because a tiny plastic latch on the dust cup snaps and no spare part is sold. Similarly, some kettles cannot be opened without breaking glued seams, making even a simple switch repair nearly impossible.

Consumer advocacy groups and engineering schools have started using this shared data in constructive ways. Design instructors assign students to examine broken appliances from repair logs and redesign weak joints or sealed casings so they can be unscrewed with standard household tools. Meanwhile, policy discussions in several countries now reference repair-cafe statistics when proposing rules that require manufacturers to supply basic replacement parts for a set number of years.

Manufacturers sometimes argue that sealed, lightweight designs keep production costs low and protect users from tampering with dangerous electrical components. Safety is a legitimate concern, especially with high-voltage devices. For that reason, repair advocates distinguish between parts that ordinary owners can safely swap—such as filters, batteries, and latches—and internal components that should only be serviced by certified technicians.

Ultimately, the data gathered at neighborhood tables shows that durability is shaped long before an item breaks. While volunteers can rescue individual machines one Saturday at a time, lasting waste reduction depends on feeding those hands-on lessons back into how products are engineered in the first place.
passage.translation: 多くの都市で週末に開かれる「リペアカフェ」では、壊れたトースターや照明、自転車を住民が持ち込み、技術を持つボランティアと無料で修理します。当初の目的は日用品の寿命を延ばしごみを減らすことでしたが、ここ10年で「家電がなぜ壊れるのか」という詳細な記録を生み出す場にもなっています。各地の団体が製品の種類・使用年数・故障箇所を記録して何千件も集約すると明確な傾向が見えてきます。例えばモーターは10年動くのにダストカップの小さなプラスチック留め具が2年で折れ交換部品も売られていない掃除機や、接着されていて開けると壊れるためスイッチひとつ直せない電気ケトルなどです。消費者団体や工学系の学校はこのデータを活用し、標準工具で分解できる設計演習や、一定期間の交換部品供給を義務づける政策議論に役立てています。メーカー側は密閉軽量設計の低コスト性や高電圧部への安全性を挙げますが、推進派も一般利用者が安全に交換できる部品と有資格技術者が扱う内部部品を区別しています。地域の修理台から集まった知見を最初の製品設計へ還元することが、持続的な廃棄物削減のカギを握っています。

To explain why volunteers refuse to touch cleaning devices.

小さな部品の破損と部品未供給で製品全体が廃棄される例。
モーターは10年動くとある。
ボランティアが拒否したとはない。
items.translation: 著者が第2段落でハンディ掃除機に言及しているのはなぜですか。

passage.title: Repair Cafes and How Products Are Designed
passage.text:
Across many cities, weekend "repair cafes" invite residents to bring broken toasters, lamps, and bicycles to community halls where skilled volunteers help fix them for free. Most visitors come with a practical goal: extending the life of a household item and keeping it out of the trash. Over the past decade, however, these grassroots gatherings have begun producing something else of value—detailed records of why everyday appliances fail.

Volunteers at dozens of repair groups log each item's brand, approximate age, and the specific fault they encountered. When thousands of entries are combined, clear patterns emerge. For example, a handheld vacuum might have a motor capable of running for ten years, yet be discarded after two because a tiny plastic latch on the dust cup snaps and no spare part is sold. Similarly, some kettles cannot be opened without breaking glued seams, making even a simple switch repair nearly impossible.

Consumer advocacy groups and engineering schools have started using this shared data in constructive ways. Design instructors assign students to examine broken appliances from repair logs and redesign weak joints or sealed casings so they can be unscrewed with standard household tools. Meanwhile, policy discussions in several countries now reference repair-cafe statistics when proposing rules that require manufacturers to supply basic replacement parts for a set number of years.

Manufacturers sometimes argue that sealed, lightweight designs keep production costs low and protect users from tampering with dangerous electrical components. Safety is a legitimate concern, especially with high-voltage devices. For that reason, repair advocates distinguish between parts that ordinary owners can safely swap—such as filters, batteries, and latches—and internal components that should only be serviced by certified technicians.

Ultimately, the data gathered at neighborhood tables shows that durability is shaped long before an item breaks. While volunteers can rescue individual machines one Saturday at a time, lasting waste reduction depends on feeding those hands-on lessons back into how products are engineered in the first place.
passage.translation: 多くの都市で週末に開かれる「リペアカフェ」では、壊れたトースターや照明、自転車を住民が持ち込み、技術を持つボランティアと無料で修理します。当初の目的は日用品の寿命を延ばしごみを減らすことでしたが、ここ10年で「家電がなぜ壊れるのか」という詳細な記録を生み出す場にもなっています。各地の団体が製品の種類・使用年数・故障箇所を記録して何千件も集約すると明確な傾向が見えてきます。例えばモーターは10年動くのにダストカップの小さなプラスチック留め具が2年で折れ交換部品も売られていない掃除機や、接着されていて開けると壊れるためスイッチひとつ直せない電気ケトルなどです。消費者団体や工学系の学校はこのデータを活用し、標準工具で分解できる設計演習や、一定期間の交換部品供給を義務づける政策議論に役立てています。メーカー側は密閉軽量設計の低コスト性や高電圧部への安全性を挙げますが、推進派も一般利用者が安全に交換できる部品と有資格技術者が扱う内部部品を区別しています。地域の修理台から集まった知見を最初の製品設計へ還元することが、持続的な廃棄物削減のカギを握っています。

items.prompt: What is the main point of the final paragraph?
choices: Volunteer repairs alone can eliminate all industrial waste.
People should stop bringing broken bicycles to community halls.
Products were always easier to fix before repair cafes existed.
Long-term waste reduction requires applying repair insights to initial product design.
items.explanation: 週末ごとの個別修理だけでなく、現場で得られた知見を最初の製品設計へフィードバックすることが長期的なごみ削減に不可欠だとしている。
distractorReasons: ボランティア修理だけで全廃できるとは言っていない。
持ち込みをやめるべきとは言っていない。
過去の美化ではなく今後の設計への還元が主旨。
最終文のfeeding those hands-on lessons back into how products are engineeredと一致。
items.translation: 最終段落の要旨は何ですか。

items.prompt: The city council voted to (     ) the old warehouse district into a pedestrian-friendly arts quarter.
items.explanation: 古い倉庫街を歩行者に優しい芸術地区へ「作り変える・一変させる」transform A into B。

transformは大きく変える・改修する。intoと対応。
transplantは移植する。
transportは輸送する。

items.prompt: Because the two witnesses gave (     ) accounts of the accident, investigators checked nearby security cameras.

convincingは説得力のある（両方説得力があるだけでは再調査理由として弱い）。
conflicting accountsで食い違う説明。
cooperatingは協力している。

items.prompt: Guests with food allergies are asked to (     ) the hotel restaurant at least three days before arrival.

nominateは指名・推薦する。
negotiateは交渉する（人を直接目的語にして「知らせる」にはならない）。
nourishは栄養を与える。
items.translation: 食物アレルギーのある宿泊客は、到着の遅くとも3日前までにホテルのレストランへ知らせるよう求められています。

items.prompt: Even a minor calculation error at the beginning of the experiment can (     ) the final measurements.
items.explanation: 最初の小さな計算ミスが最終測定値を「ゆがめる・狂わせる」distort。

distributeは配る。

items.prompt: The mountain hut has limited solar power, so hikers are urged to use electricity (     ).

distractorReasons: abundantlyは豊富に（電力制限と逆）。
fiercelyは激しく。
roughlyは大ざっぱに・荒く。
sparinglyは控えめに・無駄なく。

items.prompt: Dr. Miura's lecture was praised for making complex climate models (     ) to high school students.
items.explanation: 複雑な気候モデルを高校生にも「理解しやすい・近づきやすい」ものにしたaccessible to。
distractorReasons: acceptableは受け入れられる（許容）。
accessible toで（難しい内容が）〜にも理解できる。
applicableは適用できる。
adjustableは調整可能な。

items.prompt: The ferry service will remain suspended (     ) the harbor authorities confirm that the waves have subsided.

whereasは対比。
despiteは前置詞。
items.translation: 波が収まったと港湾当局が確認するまで、フェリーの運航は見合わせのままとなります。

items.prompt: When choosing a study desk, you should take your room's lighting and chair height into (     ).
items.explanation: take A into accountで「Aを考慮に入れる」。
distractorReasons: into actionは実行に移す（put）。

take placeは開催される。
take ... into accountで考慮する。
items.translation: 学習机を選ぶときは、部屋の照明と椅子の高さを考慮に入れるべきです。

items.prompt: The coach reminded the players that consistent daily practice is no less important (     ) physical talent.
items.explanation: no less＋形容詞＋than ... で「…に劣らず重要だ」。
distractorReasons: asはas important asのときに使う。
toはinferior/superiorなどと使う。

fromは使わない。
items.translation: コーチは選手たちに、毎日の着実な練習は身体的な才能に劣らず重要だと念を押しました。

items.prompt: Several local shops agreed to (     ) the youth marathon by providing water cups and towels.
items.explanation: 紙コップやタオルを提供して青少年マラソンの「スポンサーになる・協賛する」sponsor。
distractorReasons: sponsor an eventで催しに協賛・後援する。
scatterはまき散らす。
scoldはしかる。
shrinkは縮む。

items.prompt: Having worked in three coastal towns, Ms. Aoki has firsthand (     ) of how fishing communities adapt to storms.
items.explanation: 3つの港町で働いた経験から「直接の知識・知見」を持っているのでfirsthand knowledge of。
distractorReasons: permissionは許可。
firsthand knowledge ofで直接得た知識。
appetiteは食欲。
shelterは避難場所。
items.translation: 3つの海辺の町で働いた経験があるため、青木さんは漁村が嵐にどう適応するかについて直接の知見を持っています。

items.prompt: The committee postponed its vote because the financial figures presented at the meeting were still (     ).
items.explanation: 提示された財務数値がまだ「仮のもの・暫定的」だったため採決を延期したtentative。
distractorReasons: talkativeはおしゃべりな。
tentativeは仮の・確定していない。延期理由に合致。
thoroughは徹底的な（それなら延期理由にならない）。
tameは飼いならされた・退屈な。
items.translation: 会議で示された財務の数字がまだ暫定的なものだったため、委員会は採決を延期しました。

items.prompt: New employees are paired with an experienced colleague who helps them (     ) into the workplace smoothly.
items.explanation: settle into the workplaceで「新しい職場に慣れる・落ち着く」。
distractorReasons: stumbleはつまずく。
splitは分裂する。
sweepは掃く。

items.prompt: The botanical garden asks visitors to stay on paved paths lest rare moss (     ) trampled.
items.explanation: lest＋主語＋(should)＋原形（be）で「〜しないように」。珍しいコケが踏みつけられないよう舗装路を歩く。
distractorReasons: 直説法現在isは標準文法のlest節に用いない。
過去形wasは不適。
lest節の仮定法現在で原形beを用いる。
will beは用いない。
items.translation: 植物園では、珍しいコケが踏み荒らされないよう舗装された歩道から出ないよう来園者に求めています。

items.prompt: Far from (     ) interest in print books, the town's reading festival attracted its largest crowd in ten years.
items.explanation: far from＋動名詞（losing）で「〜するどころか（それどころか逆だ）」。
distractorReasons: Far from losing interestで関心を失うどころか。
前置詞fromの後ろに原形は置けない。
過去分詞は置けない。
to不定詞は置けない。
items.translation: 紙の本への関心を失うどころか、町の読書フェスティバルはここ10年で最大の来場者を集めました。

items.prompt: Please back up your presentation files onto an external drive in the (     ) of a network outage.
items.explanation: in the event of＋名詞で「万が一〜が起きた場合には」。
distractorReasons: aspectは側面。
on behalf ofなら〜を代表して。
in the course ofは〜の過程で。

items.prompt: The new recycling bins have color-coded lids that correspond (     ) the symbols printed on product labels.
items.explanation: correspond toで「〜に対応する・一致する」。
distractorReasons: correspond to the symbolsで記号に対応している。
atは使わない。
ofは使わない。
forは使わない。
items.translation: 新しいリサイクル回収箱には、製品ラベルに印刷された記号に対応する色分けされたふたが付いています。

items.prompt: 空所(18)を補ってください。
items.explanation: 下向きフードと暖色化に加え、さらに深夜の人感センサー減光も導入したという追加説明。
distractorReasons: 前の文を否定していない。
In additionは「さらに・加えて」。
さもないと、ではない。
逆接ではない。
items.translation: 空所(18)の補充。

passage.title: Rethinking Nighttime Lighting in Parks
passage.text:
Bright streetlamps have long been installed in urban parks to help pedestrians see footpaths and feel secure after sunset. In recent years, however, ecologists and lighting engineers have pointed out an unintended side effect: unshielded white lamps scatter glare into surrounding trees and ponds, disrupting nocturnal insects, bats, and roosting birds.

When a riverside town decided to replace its aging park lamps, officials initially assumed they had to choose between human safety and wildlife protection. Turning lights off completely made evening joggers uneasy. Yet consultations with lighting specialists revealed a third approach. By fitting hoods that directed light strictly downward and shifting from harsh blue-white LEDs to warmer amber tones, the town could keep paths clearly visible while leaving tree canopies dark. (18), motion sensors dimmed secondary trails late at night when nobody was walking past.

Six months after the upgrade, insect surveys along the riverbank showed a marked recovery in moth diversity compared with brightly lit neighboring streets. Residents also responded positively; many noted that shielded lamps actually made it easier to see obstacles on the ground because (19).

The project demonstrated that environmental care does not always demand giving up public convenience. Often, the real problem lies in wasted energy—in this case, light shining into the sky where no walker needs it. Careful design allowed the park to (20).
passage.translation: 都市の公園では日没後の歩行者の安全のため明るい街灯が設置されてきましたが、近年は覆いのない白い光が周囲の樹木や池に漏れ、夜行性の昆虫やコウモリ、眠る鳥に悪影響を与えることが指摘されています。ある川沿いの町が古い街灯を更新する際、当初は「人の安全か野生生物の保護か」の二択だと思われ、完全消灯には夜間のランナーから不安が出ました。しかし照明の専門家と相談し、光を真下だけに絞るフードを付け、青白いLEDから温かみのある琥珀色に変えることで、樹冠を暗く保ちつつ歩道をはっきり照らす第3の方法が見つかりました。(18)、深夜に人が通らない小道では人感センサーで減光しました。半年後の調査では川辺のガの多様性が回復し、住民からも(19)ため地面の障害物がかえって見やすくなったと好評でした。環境配慮は必ずしも利便性の犠牲を求めるわけではなく、空へ漏れる無駄な光をなくす設計によって公園は(20)ことができました。

items.prompt: 空所(19)を補ってください。
choices: all footpaths had been covered with white paint
joggers were required to carry heavy lanterns
glare was no longer shining directly into pedestrians' eyes
trees along the river had been cut down
items.explanation: 覆い付きランプにしたことで足元が見やすくなった光学的理由。
distractorReasons: 歩道を白く塗ったとはない。
ランタン持参の義務はない。
まぶしい光が歩行者の目に直接入らなくなったため。
木を切ったのでは樹冠を暗く保った話と矛盾。
items.translation: 空所(19)の補充。

passage.title: Why Recipes Sometimes Fail at High Altitude
passage.text:
Travelers staying in a mountain cabin two thousand meters above sea level are often puzzled when a familiar family recipe turns out strangely. Spaghetti takes longer to soften in boiling water, while a sponge cake that rises beautifully near the coast may puff up too fast in the oven and then collapse in the middle.

The cause is lower atmospheric pressure. At sea level, the weight of the air above pushes down on a pot of water, keeping molecules in liquid form until the temperature reaches 100 degrees Celsius. High in the mountains, thinner air exerts less pressure, so water begins boiling at around 93 degrees. Turning up the stove flame only produces more steam; it cannot make the boiling water any hotter. (21), foods cooked by boiling simply need extra minutes to finish.

Baking involves the same physics in reverse. Bubbles of steam and gas inside cake batter expand more forcefully when external air pressure is weak. Before the flour and eggs have time to set into a firm structure, the batter stretches too thin and sinks. Experienced mountain bakers compensate by reducing leavening powder slightly and raising oven temperature a little so the structure firms up sooner. (22), adding a spoonful of extra liquid prevents the batter from drying out in thin, dry mountain air.

Understanding these adjustments turns kitchen frustration into a practical science lesson. A recipe written in a coastal city assumes invisible environmental conditions. Once cooks recognize (23), they can adapt their methods confidently wherever they travel.

passage.title: Borrowing Tablets for the Field Survey
passage.text:
From: Mr. Watanabe, Geography Department
To: Fieldwork Group Leaders
Subject: Tablet checkout and offline maps for Thursday

Hello group leaders,
For Thursday's land-use survey around Kawagoe District, each group will receive one school tablet preloaded with our mapping app. Because mobile data reception can be weak near the old canal, you must download your assigned sector's offline map onto the tablet before leaving campus. Come to the geography prep room during Wednesday lunch break to check out your device and complete the download over school Wi-Fi.

During the survey, use the app to mark building types and photograph street signs, but avoid photographing private house nameplates or pedestrians' faces. Each tablet comes with a shoulder strap; whoever is carrying the device must wear the strap at all times when walking near water.

All groups must return to school by 3:45 p.m. so data can be backed up before club activities begin at 4:15 p.m. Do not delete accidental photos in the field—you might erase shared group pins by mistake. We will sort the files together back in the classroom.

Regards,
K. Watanabe
passage.translation: 地理科の渡辺先生からフィールドワーク班長への連絡。木曜の川越地区土地利用調査では地図アプリ入りの学校タブレットを各班1台貸し出す。旧運河付近は電波が弱いことがあるため、出発前に担当区画のオフライン地図をダウンロードしておく必要がある。水曜の昼休みに地理準備室へ来て端末を受け取り、校内Wi-Fiでダウンロードを済ませること。調査中は建物の種類を記録し道路標識を撮影するが、個人宅の表札や歩行者の顔は写さないこと。水辺を歩く際は落下防止のため付属のショルダーストラップを必ず着用すること。4時15分の部活動開始前にデータをバックアップするため午後3時45分までに帰校すること。共有ピンを誤消去する恐れがあるため現地で失敗写真を削除せず、帰校後に教室で一緒に整理する。

passage.title: How Libraries Handle Returned Books Behind the Scenes
passage.text:
When library patrons slip a borrowed novel through a return slot, their part of the transaction takes two seconds. Behind the wall, however, getting thousands of returned items back onto the exact shelves where the next reader can find them is a logistical challenge. Even a book placed two shelves away from its call number is effectively lost until someone spots it during a manual shelf check.

Many large public libraries have adopted radio-frequency identification, or RFID, tags—thin stickers with tiny antennas placed inside book covers—paired with conveyor belts that sort returned items into bins by floor and subject. Automation speeds up check-in and reduces repetitive strain on staff wrists. Yet technology alone has not made human judgment unnecessary.

Machines cannot easily tell whether a picture book has a torn page, whether a travel guide is missing its fold-out map, or whether rain has dampened the corners of a textbook. Staff still inspect items as they come out of the bins, setting aside damaged volumes for tape repair or drying before mildew can spread to neighboring books on the shelf. In addition, librarians watch which topics return in waves—such as gardening in April or tax guides in February—and place popular returns on front display tables rather than sending them straight to distant stacks.

Smaller branch libraries without conveyor systems rely on simple workflow rules instead. Returned books are first arranged in exact order on wheeled carts before anyone walks into the reading room, cutting shelving time in half and keeping aisles clear for visitors. New student assistants are also asked to shelve for only thirty minutes at a stretch, because fatigue sharply increases misplacement mistakes.

Whether a library uses sensor-guided belts or hand-pushed carts, accuracy depends on combining reliable routines with attentive human eyes. A catalog is useful only when the physical book is actually waiting where the screen says it is.
passage.translation: 利用者が返却ポストに本を入れるのはわずか2秒ですが、壁の向こうで何千冊もの返却本を次の読み手が見つけられる正確な棚へ戻すのは高度な物流作業です。請求記号から棚2段ずれて置かれただけでも、棚点検で見つかるまで実質的に行方不明になるからです。多くの大規模図書館では表紙裏の薄いRFIDタグとベルトコンベヤーを組み合わせ、階や分野ごとに自動仕分けして返却処理の迅速化と職員の手首の負担軽減を図っています。しかし機械だけでは人間の判断は不要になりません。絵本の破れや旅行ガイドの折り込み地図の欠落、雨によるページの湿りは機械では見抜きにくく、職員が点検して補修や乾燥を行い棚の他の本へのカビ拡大を防ぎます。また4月の園芸や2月の確定申告など季節ごとに動く本を見極め、奥の書架ではなく正面の展示台へ並べる工夫も人が担います。自動設備のない小規模分館でも、カート上で厳密に並べてから書架へ向かう手順や、疲労による配架ミスを防ぐため学生補助員の連続配架を30分に区切るルールが精度を支えています。どれほど設備が異なっても、画面上の蔵書検索が役立つのは実物の本が正しい場所に置かれていてこそなのです。

passage.title: How Libraries Handle Returned Books Behind the Scenes
passage.text:
When library patrons slip a borrowed novel through a return slot, their part of the transaction takes two seconds. Behind the wall, however, getting thousands of returned items back onto the exact shelves where the next reader can find them is a logistical challenge. Even a book placed two shelves away from its call number is effectively lost until someone spots it during a manual shelf check.

Many large public libraries have adopted radio-frequency identification, or RFID, tags—thin stickers with tiny antennas placed inside book covers—paired with conveyor belts that sort returned items into bins by floor and subject. Automation speeds up check-in and reduces repetitive strain on staff wrists. Yet technology alone has not made human judgment unnecessary.

Machines cannot easily tell whether a picture book has a torn page, whether a travel guide is missing its fold-out map, or whether rain has dampened the corners of a textbook. Staff still inspect items as they come out of the bins, setting aside damaged volumes for tape repair or drying before mildew can spread to neighboring books on the shelf. In addition, librarians watch which topics return in waves—such as gardening in April or tax guides in February—and place popular returns on front display tables rather than sending them straight to distant stacks.

Smaller branch libraries without conveyor systems rely on simple workflow rules instead. Returned books are first arranged in exact order on wheeled carts before anyone walks into the reading room, cutting shelving time in half and keeping aisles clear for visitors. New student assistants are also asked to shelve for only thirty minutes at a stretch, because fatigue sharply increases misplacement mistakes.

Whether a library uses sensor-guided belts or hand-pushed carts, accuracy depends on combining reliable routines with attentive human eyes. A catalog is useful only when the physical book is actually waiting where the screen says it is.

passage.title: When Saving Water Changes Habits
passage.text:
A housing cooperative fitted low-flow shower heads in its apartments. The equipment was designed to use less water each minute while still providing a comfortable shower. Based on the devices' technical specifications, the cooperative expected a substantial reduction in total water use. However, the first three months produced a smaller reduction than expected.

Interviews with residents helped explain the difference. Some people said the new shower felt pleasant and therefore stayed in it longer. Others believed the equipment made water use so small that there was little reason to worry about time. In both cases, a technical improvement had been partly offset by (18). The equipment was working as designed, but this alone did not determine the final result.

The cooperative did not remove the shower heads or blame residents for behaving badly. Instead, it shared simple information about the difference between water used per minute and water used during an entire shower. Residents were also given a way to see their own household's weekly use, rather than compare themselves with a single average household. (19), a family with several children would naturally use more water than someone living alone.

Later results suggested that combining efficient equipment with understandable feedback was more useful than relying on equipment alone. The lesson was not that efficient technology has no value. Rather, organizations should (20) when estimating its benefits. A device can make conservation easier, but the choices people make around it remain important.

passage.title: The Value of an Unfinished List
passage.text:
A coastal town began recording the wildlife found in its public gardens. Volunteers were asked to photograph insects and upload their observations to a shared website. The project attracted many enthusiastic participants, and its first map appeared to show that the central park had far more kinds of insects than any other garden. Some officials suggested concentrating future planting there.

A coordinator examined the observation records more carefully. The central park was close to a bus stop and had a popular cafe, so volunteers visited it frequently. Several smaller gardens had been visited only once. The map therefore reflected not only where insects lived but also (21). Treating every blank area on the map as an absence of wildlife would have been misleading.

The coordinator arranged visits to the less popular gardens and asked participants to spend a similar amount of time at each location. Specialists helped check photographs of insects that were difficult to identify. The revised map still had gaps, but the team marked these openly rather than filling them with guesses. (22), users could distinguish between an area where few insects had been seen and an area that had not yet been studied adequately.

The town eventually used the record to plan a wider network of flowering plants across its gardens. It did not wait until the list contained every possible species. Nevertheless, officials learned to treat the map as a developing source of evidence, not a complete picture. The project's usefulness depended on (23). A visually impressive map was valuable only if its limits were understood.

passage.title: Trial of the Flexible Workspace
passage.text:
From: Priya Shah, Facilities Manager
To: Staff in the West Building
Subject: Four-week workspace trial

Dear colleagues,
From next Monday, the third-floor meeting room will be used as a quiet workspace during the morning. This is a four-week trial, not a permanent change. Staff feedback has shown that some tasks require longer periods without interruption than our open office currently allows. The room will remain available for meetings after 1 p.m.

You may reserve a desk through the internal booking page up to two working days ahead. To give more people a chance to participate, please book no more than two mornings per week. If you no longer need a booking, cancel it promptly. Desks cannot be reserved by leaving personal belongings overnight.

During the trial, the room is intended for individual work. Please take telephone and video calls elsewhere, even if you use headphones. There will be no charge to your department for using the room. However, this does not include printing costs, which will continue to be charged in the usual way.

We will record how often desks are used, but the number of bookings will not be our only measure of success. At the end of the trial, participants and their team leaders will be asked whether the arrangement helped them complete suitable tasks and whether it created difficulties for their teams. We also want to hear from staff who wanted to participate but could not find a suitable time.

Please do not assume that the booking rules will remain unchanged after the trial. They will be reviewed along with the room's future use. Send any urgent concerns directly to me rather than waiting for the final survey.

Priya

passage.title: A Space for the River
passage.text:
For many years, the people of Bellford regarded their river mainly as a threat. High walls separated it from nearby streets, and a narrow channel carried water quickly through the center of town. The design had protected buildings during many ordinary storms. However, as the town expanded, more roofs and paved surfaces prevented rain from soaking into the ground. Water reached the river faster, and maintaining safety became increasingly difficult.

One response would have been to make the walls higher. Instead, planners proposed allowing the river more room at a former industrial site upstream. Old warehouses there had been removed, leaving land that could temporarily hold water during heavy rain. In dry weather, most of the area could be used as a public park. The proposal did not eliminate the need for walls elsewhere; it was intended to complement existing defenses.

Some residents objected that a park designed to flood was a waste of money. They feared that equipment would be damaged and the area would be closed too often. The design team responded by placing expensive electrical equipment above expected water levels and choosing surfaces that could be cleaned after flooding. Path signs explained that lower routes might close, while a higher route would remain available under most conditions.

A more difficult question concerned who would benefit. The park was near a neighborhood with few green spaces, but many people living there had not attended the early planning meetings. The meetings had been held during working hours and relied on technical presentations. The town changed the schedule and used a temporary model that residents could walk around. This led to requests for better lighting, places to sit, and a safer crossing to the park.

After the park opened, a severe storm tested the design. Water spread across the lower ground as intended, and some paths were closed for cleaning afterward. Officials resisted describing this as a failure of the park: temporary flooding was part of its protective function. At the same time, they acknowledged that the cleanup had taken longer than expected and revised the maintenance plan.

Bellford's experience illustrates why adapting to floods involves more than building a single structure. The physical design, the ability to maintain it, and the ways people understand and use it all matter. A project can serve several purposes, but those purposes need to be explained honestly. Calling a floodable park permanently dry would create false expectations; treating it only as empty storage would overlook its everyday value to residents.
passage.translation: ベルフォードでは高い壁と狭い水路で川を制御してきましたが、市街化で雨水の地下浸透が減り、流入が速くなって安全確保が難しくなりました。壁を高くする代わりに、上流の旧工業用地を大雨時の貯水空間にし、通常は公園として使う案が出ました。既存の防御をなくすのでなく補完する計画です。設備の損傷や閉鎖への懸念には、電気設備の高所設置や清掃しやすい舗装、低い道の閉鎖表示と高い道の確保で対応しました。緑地の少ない近隣住民が初期会合に少なかったのは、勤務時間中の開催と技術的説明が原因でした。時間変更と歩いて見られる模型により、照明、椅子、安全な横断路の希望が集まりました。開園後の大雨では計画どおり低地に水が広がり、その後清掃のため道が閉じられました。行政は洪水自体を失敗とはしませんでしたが、清掃に想定以上の時間がかかったことは認め管理計画を改めました。物理的設計、維持能力、住民の理解と利用がいずれも重要です。多目的な施設の目的を正直に説明すべきで、常に乾燥した公園と呼ぶのも、単なる空の貯水場と見るのも適切ではありません。

倉庫は除去済みで工業利用に戻さない。
items.translation: 新しい公園の役割は何ですか。

passage.title: A Space for the River
passage.text:
For many years, the people of Bellford regarded their river mainly as a threat. High walls separated it from nearby streets, and a narrow channel carried water quickly through the center of town. The design had protected buildings during many ordinary storms. However, as the town expanded, more roofs and paved surfaces prevented rain from soaking into the ground. Water reached the river faster, and maintaining safety became increasingly difficult.

One response would have been to make the walls higher. Instead, planners proposed allowing the river more room at a former industrial site upstream. Old warehouses there had been removed, leaving land that could temporarily hold water during heavy rain. In dry weather, most of the area could be used as a public park. The proposal did not eliminate the need for walls elsewhere; it was intended to complement existing defenses.

Some residents objected that a park designed to flood was a waste of money. They feared that equipment would be damaged and the area would be closed too often. The design team responded by placing expensive electrical equipment above expected water levels and choosing surfaces that could be cleaned after flooding. Path signs explained that lower routes might close, while a higher route would remain available under most conditions.

A more difficult question concerned who would benefit. The park was near a neighborhood with few green spaces, but many people living there had not attended the early planning meetings. The meetings had been held during working hours and relied on technical presentations. The town changed the schedule and used a temporary model that residents could walk around. This led to requests for better lighting, places to sit, and a safer crossing to the park.

After the park opened, a severe storm tested the design. Water spread across the lower ground as intended, and some paths were closed for cleaning afterward. Officials resisted describing this as a failure of the park: temporary flooding was part of its protective function. At the same time, they acknowledged that the cleanup had taken longer than expected and revised the maintenance plan.

Bellford's experience illustrates why adapting to floods involves more than building a single structure. The physical design, the ability to maintain it, and the ways people understand and use it all matter. A project can serve several purposes, but those purposes need to be explained honestly. Calling a floodable park permanently dry would create false expectations; treating it only as empty storage would overlook its everyday value to residents.
passage.translation: ベルフォードでは高い壁と狭い水路で川を制御してきましたが、市街化で雨水の地下浸透が減り、流入が速くなって安全確保が難しくなりました。壁を高くする代わりに、上流の旧工業用地を大雨時の貯水空間にし、通常は公園として使う案が出ました。既存の防御をなくすのでなく補完する計画です。設備の損傷や閉鎖への懸念には、電気設備の高所設置や清掃しやすい舗装、低い道の閉鎖表示と高い道の確保で対応しました。緑地の少ない近隣住民が初期会合に少なかったのは、勤務時間中の開催と技術的説明が原因でした。時間変更と歩いて見られる模型により、照明、椅子、安全な横断路の希望が集まりました。開園後の大雨では計画どおり低地に水が広がり、その後清掃のため道が閉じられました。行政は洪水自体を失敗とはしませんでしたが、清掃に想定以上の時間がかかったことは認め管理計画を改めました。物理的設計、維持能力、住民の理解と利用がいずれも重要です。多目的な施設の目的を正直に説明すべきで、常に乾燥した公園と呼ぶのも、単なる空の貯水場と見るのも適切ではありません。

items.prompt: Why did the town change its public meetings?
choices: Residents had asked for more technical language.
The model had been damaged during a flood.
The original format had excluded some nearby residents in practice.
Officials wanted to avoid questions about safety.
items.explanation: 勤務時間中と難しい説明で、必要な近隣住民が参加しにくかった。
distractorReasons: むしろ説明を理解しやすく変えた。
模型破損はない。
参加障壁を減らす変更だった。
安全への要望にも対応するため。
items.translation: 住民会合を変更した理由は何ですか。

items.prompt: How did officials respond after the severe storm?
choices: They announced that no further maintenance was necessary.
They closed the park permanently because water entered it.
They denied that cleaning had caused any difficulty.
They distinguished intended flooding from a maintenance problem that needed improvement.
items.explanation: 想定内の浸水は失敗でなく、清掃の遅れは改善対象と分けた。
distractorReasons: 管理計画を改定した。
閉鎖は清掃のための一時的なもの。
時間超過は認めている。
保護機能と実務上の課題を区別した。
items.translation: 大雨後の行政の対応はどうでしたか。

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the article's conclusion?
choices: Successful adaptation requires design, maintenance, participation, and honest explanation of functions.
A floodable park is useful only when it contains no visitors.
Technical structures make public understanding unnecessary.
Projects serving more than one purpose should always be rejected.
items.explanation: 設計、維持、利用者の理解、多目的性の正確な説明が結論。
distractorReasons: 最後の段落の主要要素を統合する。
日常の住民への価値を認めている。
理解も重要と明記。
多目的性自体は否定していない。
items.translation: 本文の結論に最も近いものはどれですか。

items.prompt: The city council approved a plan to (     ) the abandoned tram depot into an indoor farmers' market.
items.explanation: 使われなくなった路面電車の車庫を屋内市場へ「改修する」のでrenovate。
distractorReasons: retaliateは報復する。
renovateは建物などを改修・改装する。
replicateは複製・再現する。
reprimandは叱責する。
items.translation: 市議会は使われなくなった路面電車の車庫を屋内ファーマーズマーケットに改修する計画を承認しました。

items.prompt: Because the ferry harbor is shallow at low tide, large vessels are (     ) from entering after 4 p.m.
items.explanation: prohibit A from doingで「Aが〜するのを禁止する」。干潮で浅くなるため大型船の進入を禁じる。
distractorReasons: persuadeはto不定詞を伴い説得する。
promoteは促進する。
preserveは保存する。
prohibited ... from enteringで入港を禁止されている。
items.translation: 干潮時はフェリー港が浅くなるため、午後4時以降は大型船の入港が禁止されています。

items.prompt: Although the new packaging looks identical to plastic, it is designed to (     ) naturally in soil within months.
items.explanation: 数か月以内に土の中で自然に「分解する」ように設計された素材なのでdecompose。
distractorReasons: decomposeは有機物や生分解素材が分解する。
disappearだけでは生物・化学的分解の仕組みとしてdecomposeほど的確ではない。
distributeは配布する。
distinguishは区別する。
items.translation: その新しい包装材は見た目はプラスチックとそっくりですが、数か月以内に土の中で自然分解するよう作られています。

items.prompt: The orchestra's outdoor performance was postponed (     ) sudden gusts of wind that blew music stands over.
items.explanation: 譜面台を倒す突風「が原因で」延期されたのでon account of。
distractorReasons: in contrast toは〜と対照的に。
on behalf ofは〜を代表して。
on account of＋名詞で「〜のために・が原因で」。
in spite ofは〜にもかかわらず（延期と逆）。
items.translation: 譜面台を吹き飛ばす突風のため、オーケストラの野外公演は延期されました。

items.prompt: Before signing a lease on an old building, prospective shop owners should have the electrical wiring thoroughly (     ).
items.explanation: 古い建物の賃貸契約を結ぶ前に電気配線を徹底的に「点検してもらう」have＋O＋過去分詞inspected。
distractorReasons: inhabitedは居住された。
inflictedは（損害などを）与えられた。
insertedは挿入された。
inspectedは点検された。
items.translation: 古い建物の賃貸契約に署名する前に、出店希望者は電気配線を徹底的に点検してもらうべきです。

items.prompt: Many commuters remain (     ) about whether adding one extra bus per hour will noticeably ease morning crowding.
items.explanation: 1時間に1本増便するだけで朝の混雑が目に見えて緩和するか「懐疑的だ」skeptical about。
distractorReasons: sympatheticは同情的な。
skepticalは疑わしく思っている・懐疑的な。
spontaneousは自発的な。
subordinateは下位の。
items.translation: 1時間にバスを1本増やすだけで朝の混雑が目立って緩和するかどうか、多くの通勤客は依然として懐疑的です。

items.prompt: The university museum grants free admission to local high school students as a (     ) of goodwill toward the neighborhood.
items.explanation: a gesture of goodwillで「善意の表れ・計らい」。
distractorReasons: glimpseはちらりと見えること。
garmentは衣類。
gestureは気持ちを表す行為・計らい。
gravityは重力・重大さ。
items.translation: 大学博物館は近隣地域への善意の計らいとして、地元の高校生を無料入館にしています。

items.prompt: Had the hikers checked the ridge weather bulletin at dawn, they (     ) caught in the afternoon hailstorm.
items.explanation: 過去の事実に反する仮定法過去完了の倒置（Had＋S＋過去分詞）に対する帰結節would not have been。
distractorReasons: 仮定法過去完了の主節かつ受動態would not have been caught。
単純未来で時制が合わない。
主節にhad not beenは使わない。
現在形で合わない。
items.translation: もし登山者たちが夜明けに尾根の気象情報を確認していたら、午後のひょう嵐に遭わずに済んだでしょう。

items.prompt: Small coastal bakeries have struggled to absorb the (     ) rise in butter and wheat prices over the past two years.
items.explanation: 価格の「急激な・大幅な」上昇を表すsteep rise。
distractorReasons: shallowは浅い。
scarceは乏しい（上昇の程度には使わない）。
steep riseで急激な上昇。
solemnは厳粛な。
items.translation: 海辺の小さなパン屋は、過去2年間のバターと小麦価格の急騰を吸収するのに苦心してきました。

items.prompt: Once you submit the online application, an automated email will be sent to (     ) receipt of your documents.
items.explanation: acknowledge receipt of ... で「…の受領を確認・通知する」。
distractorReasons: accumulateは蓄積する。
accompanyは同行する。
accomplishは成し遂げる。
acknowledge receiptで受け取った旨を知らせる。
items.translation: オンライン申請を送信すると、書類の受領を知らせる自動メールが送られます。

items.prompt: The two research teams arrived at virtually identical conclusions completely (     ) of each other.
items.explanation: independently of each otherで「お互いにまったく独立して（連絡を取り合わずに）」。
distractorReasons: indifferentlyは無関心に。
independently ofで〜とは無関係に・独自に。
indefinitelyは無期限に。
indirectlyは間接的に（of each otherと結びつかない）。
items.translation: 2つの研究チームは互いにまったく独立して、実質的に同じ結論にたどり着きました。

items.prompt: Residents near the stadium complained that illegal street parking had become a (     ) problem on match days.
items.explanation: 試合日の路上駐車が「慢性的な・長引く」問題になったchronic problem。
distractorReasons: chronicは慢性的な・常態化した。
courteousは礼儀正しい。
compactは小型の。
compatibleは両立できる。
items.translation: 競技場近くの住民は、試合日の違法路上駐車が慢性的な問題になっていると苦情を述べました。

items.prompt: The apprentice carpenter watched closely so as not to (     ) any subtle movement of the master's chisel.
items.explanation: 師匠のノミのわずかな動きも「見落とさない」よう注意深く見たoverlook。
distractorReasons: overtakeは追い越す。
overcomeは克服する。
overflowはあふれる。
overlookは見落とす・見逃す。
items.translation: 見習い大工は、親方のノミのわずかな動きも見落とさないようじっと観察しました。

items.prompt: Although the software update includes dozens of minor tweaks, its chief (     ) is much faster file searching.
items.explanation: 細かい調整がたくさんあるが、主な「長所・利点」は検索の高速化だ、なのでmerit。
distractorReasons: marginは余白・差。
motiveは動機（ソフト自身の性質には不自然）。
meritは長所・利点。
menaceは脅威。
items.translation: 今回のソフトウェア更新には何十もの細かい調整が含まれますが、最大の長所はファイル検索が大幅に速くなったことです。

items.prompt: Volunteers planted deep-rooted grasses along the slope to keep heavy autumn rain from (     ) the soil.
items.explanation: keep A from doingの構文で、大雨が土壌を「浸食する・削り取る」のを防ぐeroding。
distractorReasons: erodeは土や岸を浸食する。
eruptは噴火する（自動詞）。
enrollは登録する。
endureは耐える。
items.translation: ボランティアたちは秋の豪雨で土が削り取られるのを防ぐため、斜面に根の深い草を植えました。

items.prompt: Strict safety rules apply to everyone in the pottery studio, be they seasoned instructors or (     ) beginners.
items.explanation: seasoned instructors（熟練指導者）との対比で「まったくの初心者」complete beginners。
distractorReasons: novice beginnersは意味が重複する。
complete beginnersは「まったくの初心者」を表す自然なコロケーション。
humbleは謙虚な。
vacantは空いている。
items.translation: 陶芸工房では、熟練の指導者であれまったくの初心者であれ、全員に厳しい安全規則が適用されます。

items.prompt: The town's disaster drill revealed that backup radios were (     ) when mobile networks became congested.
items.explanation: 携帯通信網が混雑した際、予備の無線機が「不可欠である」と分かったindispensable。
distractorReasons: inconsiderateは思いやりがない。
indispensableは必要不可欠な。

passage.title: Why Small Bridges Disappear Quietly
passage.text:
Major suspension bridges attract photographers and generous maintenance budgets, yet rural road networks depend far more on thousands of short concrete and timber spans crossing narrow streams. Most drivers pass over them without noticing. Ironically, that invisibility makes routine upkeep harder to fund until serious wear sets in.

In one mountainous prefecture, inspecting every minor bridge with large crane trucks was straining town finances. Rather than lengthening intervals between checks, the prefecture trained local road crews to use compact poles fitted with cameras and mirrors. Crews photographed the underside of short spans from the riverbank and sent the images to structural engineers at headquarters. (18), specialists spent their limited travel time visiting only bridges whose photos showed early cracks or rust.

Equally effective was clearing fallen leaves and gravel from deck drains every autumn. When drains clog, rainwater pools and seeps into joints during winter freezes, accelerating corrosion. Teaching local teams what to clear before winter cost very little, yet it (19).

passage.title: When Menu Descriptions Shape Food Waste
passage.text:
Restaurants frequently look to portion sizes when trying to cut plate waste, yet how a dish is described on a menu can be just as influential. Diners often order an unfamiliar item based on an appealing title, only to leave half of it untouched upon discovering a strong herb, a spicy sauce, or an unexpected texture.

A university dining hall tested this idea after noticing that trays returning from lunch lines carried large amounts of uneaten vegetable stews. Interviews showed that students were not opposed to plant-based dishes; rather, poetic menu names such as "Autumn Harvest Bowl" gave no clue that the dish contained bitter greens and coriander. Staff rewrote the labels to highlight sensory details—for example, "Roasted Squash Bowl with Crisp Bitter Greens and Lemon-Herb Dressing"—and placed tiny tasting spoons at the counter. (21), plate waste from featured stews fell by nearly a third within a month.

Clearer descriptions also reduced pressure during peak lunch minutes. Previously, servers spent time answering repetitive ingredient questions while the queue grew impatient. With key flavors and common allergens stated plainly at eye level, students decided faster before reaching the counter. (22), the tasting spoons encouraged hesitant diners to try unfamiliar seasonings without risking a full serving they might dislike.

The dining team concluded that reducing waste did not require shrinking meals or limiting variety. Often, waste occurred simply because (23). Giving diners honest, specific expectations helped match each plate with someone who would genuinely enjoy finishing it.
passage.translation: 飲食店が食べ残しを減らす際は量の調整に目が向きがちですが、メニューの書き方も同じくらい重要です。魅力的な料理名だけで馴染みのない品を注文し、強い香草や辛味、予想外の食感に気づいて半分残す客は少なくありません。ある大学食堂では野菜シチューの食べ残しが多い原因を調べたところ、学生は野菜料理を嫌っていたのではなく、「秋の収穫ボウル」のような詩的な名前からは苦味のある青菜やパクチーが入っていることが分からなかったと判明しました。そこで味や食感の特徴が伝わる具体的な表記に改め、カウンターに小さな試食用スプーンを置きました。(21)、1か月で対象メニューの食べ残しが約3分の1減りました。目線の高さに風味やアレルゲンが明記されたことで昼のピーク時に繰り返し質問される手間も減り、学生は列の途中で素早く決められるようになりました。(22)、試食用スプーンのおかげで迷っていた学生も一皿丸ごと残すリスクなしに新しい味付けを試せました。食べ残しの多くは単に(23)ために起きていたのであり、具体的で誠実な事前情報が完食につながったのです。

passage.title: Guidelines for the Shared Makerspace
passage.text:
From: K. Morita, Workshop Coordinator
To: Registered Makerspace Users
Subject: New 3D-printer booking system and unattended runs

Dear users,
Over the past semester, demand for our two 3D printers and laser cutter has doubled, leading to long waits before project deadlines. Starting November 1, users must upload their print file to the booking portal before reserving a time slot; the portal estimates run time automatically so nobody books a four-hour slot for a forty-minute part.

Prints lasting up to ninety minutes require you to remain in the workshop the entire time. Longer prints may run unattended during daytime hours only if you stay for the first twenty minutes to confirm that the base layer has adhered properly to the build plate—most print failures and nozzle jams occur during that initial stage. All machines shut down at 7:00 p.m. sharp; overnight printing is not permitted for fire-safety reasons.

Filament spools stored in the cabinet are shared for small prototypes under fifty grams. If your design exceeds fifty grams, please purchase a personal spool at the campus store or bring an approved PLA spool with its specification label intact. Unlabeled plastics can melt at the wrong temperature and damage the heating unit.

Best regards,
K. Morita
passage.translation: 工房コーディネーターの森田から登録利用者への連絡。前学期に3Dプリンター2台とレーザーカッターの需要が倍増し締切前に長い待ちが生じたため、11月1日から予約前に造形ファイルをポータルへアップロードする方式に変更する（所要時間を自動算出するため、40分の部品に4時間枠を取る無駄を防げる）。90分以内の造形は作業中ずっと工房内にいること。それ以上の長時間造形は、失敗やノズル詰まりの大半が起きる最初の20分間立ち会って土台層の定着を確認した場合に限り、日中の無人稼働を認める。防火安全上、午後7時に全機材を停止し夜間造形は禁止。棚の共有フィラメントは50グラム未満の試作用で、50グラムを超える場合は購買部で個人用リールを購入するか仕様ラベルが残った認定PLAリールを持参すること（ラベルなし樹脂は融点違いで加熱部を壊す恐れがある）。

items.prompt: Under what condition may a print lasting longer than ninety minutes run unattended?
choices: The user watches the first twenty minutes during daytime hours to verify base adhesion.
It starts after 7:00 p.m. and finishes before morning.
The user pays an extra fire-safety deposit at the campus store.
The part weighs more than fifty grams.
items.explanation: 日中の時間帯であり、かつ最初の20分間立ち会って土台層がプレートにしっかり定着したことを確認した場合のみ。
distractorReasons: 第2段落の条件と一致。
午後7時以降の夜間稼働は防火上禁止されている。
追加保証金の規定はない。
50グラム超は個人リールの条件であり無人稼働の条件ではない。
items.translation: 90分を超える造形を無人稼働できるのはどの条件を満たすときですか。

Their colors fade under workshop lights.
They may melt at an improper temperature and harm the heating unit.
They cannot produce parts lighter than fifty grams.
items.explanation: Unlabeled plastics can melt at the wrong temperature and damage the heating unit.と明記されている。
distractorReasons: 価格が高いからではない。
色あせが理由ではない。
不適切な温度で溶けて加熱部を損傷する恐れがあるため。
50グラム未満が作れないからではない。
items.translation: ラベルのない樹脂リールが使用禁止なのはなぜですか。

passage.title: Guidelines for the Shared Makerspace
passage.text:
From: K. Morita, Workshop Coordinator
To: Registered Makerspace Users
Subject: New 3D-printer booking system and unattended runs

Dear users,
Over the past semester, demand for our two 3D printers and laser cutter has doubled, leading to long waits before project deadlines. Starting November 1, users must upload their print file to the booking portal before reserving a time slot; the portal estimates run time automatically so nobody books a four-hour slot for a forty-minute part.

Prints lasting up to ninety minutes require you to remain in the workshop the entire time. Longer prints may run unattended during daytime hours only if you stay for the first twenty minutes to confirm that the base layer has adhered properly to the build plate—most print failures and nozzle jams occur during that initial stage. All machines shut down at 7:00 p.m. sharp; overnight printing is not permitted for fire-safety reasons.

Filament spools stored in the cabinet are shared for small prototypes under fifty grams. If your design exceeds fifty grams, please purchase a personal spool at the campus store or bring an approved PLA spool with its specification label intact. Unlabeled plastics can melt at the wrong temperature and damage the heating unit.

Best regards,
K. Morita
passage.translation: 工房コーディネーターの森田から登録利用者への連絡。前学期に3Dプリンター2台とレーザーカッターの需要が倍増し締切前に長い待ちが生じたため、11月1日から予約前に造形ファイルをポータルへアップロードする方式に変更する（所要時間を自動算出するため、40分の部品に4時間枠を取る無駄を防げる）。90分以内の造形は作業中ずっと工房内にいること。それ以上の長時間造形は、失敗やノズル詰まりの大半が起きる最初の20分間立ち会って土台層の定着を確認した場合に限り、日中の無人稼働を認める。防火安全上、午後7時に全機材を停止し夜間造形は禁止。棚の共有フィラメントは50グラム未満の試作用で、50グラムを超える場合は購買部で個人用リールを購入するか仕様ラベルが残った認定PLAリールを持参すること（ラベルなし樹脂は融点違いで加熱部を壊す恐れがある）。

items.prompt: How do modern snow-cooled warehouses maintain steady temperatures?
choices: By opening warehouse doors every night during summer.
By burying apples directly in uninsulated outdoor fields.
By spraying liquid nitrogen over wooden crates twice a day.
By using digital sensors and motorized dampers to regulate air blown past stored snow.
items.explanation: 蓄えた雪のそばを通した空気を、デジタルセンサーと電動ダンパーで制御して貯蔵室を0度付近の狭い範囲に保つ。
distractorReasons: 夏に毎晩扉を開けるのではない。
断熱のない屋外の畑に埋めるのではない。
液体窒素は使わない。
第2段落の記述と一致。
items.translation: 現代の雪冷熱倉庫はどのようにして一定の温度を保っていますか。

passage.title: Cold Storage Powered by Winter Air
passage.text:
Keeping harvested apples, potatoes, and root vegetables fresh through spring and summer requires steady, cool temperatures and high humidity. Modern warehouses achieve this with electric refrigeration, which works reliably in any climate but consumes substantial power—especially during hot months when cooling units must run hardest and electricity prices peak.

In parts of northern Japan, agricultural engineers and storage cooperatives have refined an older regional idea: capturing winter cold in massive insulated rooms filled with snow or ice blocks gathered between January and March. As outdoor temperatures climb in spring, fans circulate air past the stored snow and into adjacent produce rooms. Far from being a nostalgic curiosity, contemporary snow-cooled warehouses use digital sensors and motorized dampers to hold storage rooms within a single degree of zero Celsius.

This approach offers biological advantages alongside energy savings. Standard mechanical refrigerators cool air by passing it over subzero metal coils, a process that strips moisture from the room and can leave apples shriveled or potatoes sprouting prematurely. Air cooled by melting snow, by contrast, naturally stays above ninety percent humidity without extra humidifiers. In blind taste tests and texture measurements, certain varieties of rice, buckwheat, and root crops stored in snow rooms retain crispness and natural sweetness longer than counterparts kept in conventional chillers.

Snow cooling clearly has geographic and practical limits. Mild winters can reduce local snowfall, hauling heavy snow requires fuel, and building thick insulated chambers demands higher upfront construction spending than installing a standard compressor. Even in snowy districts, cooperatives often keep backup electric chillers for late August when stored snow finally runs low.

Still, where winter weather provides abundant snow right beside farmland, treating it as a seasonal resource rather than a road-clearing nuisance turns a costly winter burden into summer cooling capacity. The revival of snow warehouses illustrates how modern control technology can make passive, local energy sources commercially competitive.
passage.translation: 収穫したリンゴやジャガイモ、根菜を春から夏まで新鮮に保つには安定した低温と高湿度が必要ですが、一般的な電気冷蔵倉庫は猛暑期ほど大量の電力を消費します。北日本の一部では、1〜3月に集めた雪や氷を厚い断熱室に蓄え、春以降にファンで冷気を隣の貯蔵室へ送る「雪室（ゆきむろ）」の仕組みを現代技術で進化させています。単なる懐古趣味ではなく、デジタルセンサーと自動ダンパーで室温を摂氏0度前後の1度以内に精密制御します。省エネだけでなく品質面の利点もあり、氷点下の金属コイルで空気を冷やす機械式冷蔵庫は室内の水分を奪ってリンゴのしなびやジャガイモの発芽を招きやすいのに対し、溶けゆく雪で冷やされた空気は加湿器なしでも自然に湿度90%以上を保ちます。ブラインド試食や食感測定でも、米やそば、根菜のみずみずしさや自然な甘みが長く保たれることが確かめられています。もちろん暖冬による雪不足や運搬燃料、断熱倉庫の初期建設費といった制約はあり、8月下旬の雪不足に備えて補助の電気冷却機を併設する組合もあります。それでも農地のすぐ横に積もる雪を除雪の厄介者ではなく季節の資源として活かす取り組みは、現代の制御技術が自然エネルギーを商業的にも通用させる好例となっています。

items.prompt: Why do apples and root crops often stay fresher in snow-cooled rooms than in standard mechanical refrigerators?
choices: Mechanical refrigerators keep rooms above twenty degrees Celsius.
Snow-cooled air naturally keeps high humidity instead of drying produce out.
Melting snow adds artificial sugar to the skin of the fruit.
Light inside snow rooms helps potatoes continue growing leaves.
items.explanation: 機械式は金属コイルで水分を奪いやすいが、溶ける雪で冷えた空気は加湿器なしでも90%超の高湿度を自然に保つため。
distractorReasons: 機械式が20度以上になるのではない。
第3段落の水分保持の仕組みと一致。
人工の糖分を加えるのではない。
葉を伸ばさせる（発芽させる）のはむしろ防ぎたい劣化。
items.translation: 通常の機械式冷蔵庫より雪冷熱室のほうがリンゴや根菜の鮮度が保たれやすいのはなぜですか。

items.prompt: Which limitation of snow-cooled storage is acknowledged in the fourth paragraph?
choices: Digital sensors cannot function near zero degrees Celsius.
Buckwheat and rice spoil within a week in humid air.
Upfront building costs are higher and backup chillers may be needed in late summer.
Snow collected in January melts completely before April arrives.
items.explanation: 暖冬や運搬燃料、厚い断熱室の初期建設費の高さに加え、雪が減る8月下旬向けに補助の電気冷却機を備える場合がある点。
distractorReasons: センサーは第2段落で活用されている。
米やそばも品質が保たれるとある。
第4段落で挙げられた制約と一致。
4月前に全部溶けてしまうなら春夏に使えない。
items.translation: 第4段落で認められている雪冷熱貯蔵の制約はどれですか。

items.prompt: Why do some cooperatives in snowy districts still install electric chillers?
choices: Because snow rooms are illegal to operate in July.
To provide backup cooling in late August when stored snow runs low.
To freeze fresh apples solid before shipping them.
Because local farmers refuse to harvest crops in autumn.
items.explanation: 蓄えた雪がついに少なくなる8月下旬の予備冷却用として電気チラーを併設していると第4段落にある。
distractorReasons: 7月の稼働が違法とはない。
when stored snow finally runs lowへの備えと一致。
リンゴをカチカチに凍らせるためではない。
秋の収穫拒否とは無関係。
items.translation: 雪の多い地域の組合でも電気冷却機を併設することがあるのはなぜですか。

items.prompt: What broader lesson does the author draw from the revival of snow warehouses?
choices: All southern cities should import snow by truck every winter.
Electric refrigeration has no value in any climate.
Traditional farming methods work best when all modern instruments are removed.
Modern control systems can turn local, passive natural resources into practical commercial solutions.
items.explanation: 邪魔者扱いされがちな冬の雪も、現代の制御技術と組み合わせれば実用的な商業技術になるという結び。
distractorReasons: 南部の都市へトラック輸送せよとは言っていない。
機械式もあらゆる気候で確実に動くと第1段落で評価している。
現代の計測制御機器を排すべきとは言っていない。
最終文の要旨と一致。
items.translation: 雪冷熱倉庫の見直しから筆者が引き出している広い教訓は何ですか。

items.prompt: The pharmaceutical firm had to (     ) three thousand bottles of cough syrup after a labeling error was found.
items.explanation: ラベル表示の誤りが見つかったため出荷済みのシロップ3千本を「自主回収する」recall。
distractorReasons: reciteは暗唱する。
recallは製品を回収する。
recruitは募集・採用する。
recedeは後退する。
items.translation: 表示ミスが見つかったため、その製薬会社は咳止めシロップ3千本を回収せざるを得ませんでした。

items.prompt: Even minor delays at one major hub airport can have a (     ) effect on flight schedules across the country.
items.explanation: 1つの拠点空港の小さな遅れが全国の運航日程に「波及効果」を及ぼすhave a ripple effect on。
distractorReasons: rigidは硬直した。
randomは無作為な。
ripple effectで波紋・波及効果。

passage.title: Designing Hospital Signs Under Stress
passage.text:
Designing directional signs for an airport or mall is challenging, yet hospitals present an even stricter test. Visitors arriving for urgent appointments are often anxious, tired, or unfamiliar with medical terms. A sign pointing to "Otolaryngology" may be technically exact while leaving an elderly patient standing helplessly in the lobby.

When a regional medical center renovated its main building, planners shadowed first-time visitors from the bus stop to exam rooms. People rarely read long wall directories from top to bottom; instead, they looked for one simple cue at each junction. Pairing formal department names with everyday terms—such as "Ear, Nose & Throat"—immediately reduced hesitation. (18), colored stripes along the baseboard reassured visitors that they were still on the right path.

Testing also revealed a placement flaw. Designers had hung overhead panels near the ceiling, yet people pushing wheelchairs or strollers looked straight ahead and walked right under them. Lowering markers to eye level on corner pillars solved the problem. (19), consistent icons—such as a teacup for the cafeteria and a mortar for the pharmacy—helped residents still learning the local language.

Arriving without getting lost lowered visitors' stress before they met a doctor, proving that (20).
passage.translation: 空港や商業施設の案内標識も難しい仕事ですが、病院はさらに厳しい条件を突きつけます。急な受診で訪れる患者や家族は不安や疲労を抱え、専門的な診療科名になじみがないことも少なくありません。ある地域医療センターは本館改修にあたり、バス停から診察室まで初来院者に同行調査を行いました。不安な来院者は長い案内板を上から下まで読むことは少なく、曲がり角ごとに単純な手がかりを探し、分岐点では床を見る傾向がありました。そこで正式名称の横に「耳・鼻・のど」のような日常語を併記すると迷いが減りました。(18)、巾木に沿って連続する色帯を引くことで標識と標識の間も正しい道にいる安心感が生まれました。また天井近くの美しい吊り看板は、車いすやベビーカーを押して目線の高さを見る人には見落とされがちだと分かり、角の柱の目線位置に補助表示を下げました。(19)、共通アイコンの追加は地域の言語を習得中の住民の助けにもなりました。迷わず診察室に着けることは来院者の診察前の緊張を和らげ、(20)ことを実証しました。
